24020.q: What did the Greek word that our word “school” comes from mean?
24020.e: The Greek word “scholē” means free time. Only people who had time and did not have to work could learn.
24020.m: “School” comes from the Greek word for free time.

24021.q: What was a trireme mainly built from?
24021.e: Triremes were built of wood, which made them light and fast. Only the ram at the front was made of metal.
24021.m: Triremes were light ships made of wood.

24022.q: What did the Pythia sit on when she made prophecies?
24022.e: The Pythia sat on a tall stool with three legs, a tripod. She is shown like this on old vases too.
24022.m: The Pythia sat on a tripod.

24023.q: In which part of Greece is Mount Olympus?
24023.e: Mount Olympus is in the north of Greece, not far from the sea, between the regions of Thessaly and Macedonia.
24023.m: Olympus is in the north of Greece.

24024.q: According to legend, what did the gods on Olympus drink?
24024.e: According to legend, the gods drank nectar. Like their food, it was meant to keep them young for ever.
24024.m: The drink of the gods is called nectar.

24025.q: According to legend, how many great gods lived on Olympus?
24025.e: The Greeks told of twelve great gods on Olympus. Their king was Zeus.
24025.m: Twelve great gods lived on Olympus.

24026.q: What has the area around Mount Olympus been since 1938?
24026.e: In 1938 the area around Olympus became Greece’s first national park. Plants and animals are protected there.
24026.m: Greece’s first national park is at Olympus.

24027.q: Which shape does the famous Pythagoras’ theorem apply to?
24027.e: Pythagoras’ theorem applies to triangles with a right angle. It is named after Pythagoras but was known even earlier.
24027.m: Pythagoras’ theorem applies to right-angled triangles.

24028.q: An amphora is a large clay jar. Who made jars like this?
24028.e: Amphorae were shaped by potters on a potter’s wheel and then fired.

24029.q: What were the thermae in ancient Rome?
24029.e: The thermae were public baths. Many Romans bathed there almost every day.
24029.m: The thermae were the Romans’ large bathhouses.

24030.q: What was the hot room in the Roman baths called?
24030.e: In the caldarium the water was hot and the air was warm and damp. The word comes from the Latin “calidus”, meaning hot.
24030.m: The caldarium was the hottest room in the baths.

24031.q: What was there in the frigidarium of the baths?
24031.e: The frigidarium was the cold room. People cooled down there after their warm bath.
24031.m: In the frigidarium people bathed in cold water.

24032.q: What was the lukewarm room between hot and cold called?
24032.e: In the tepidarium it was pleasantly lukewarm. This way the body slowly got used to the heat.
24032.m: The tepidarium was the lukewarm room of the baths.

24033.q: What did the Romans use in the baths to scrape oil and dirt off their skin?
24033.e: The Romans hardly knew soap. They rubbed themselves with oil and scraped it off again with a curved scraper called a strigil.
24033.m: The Romans cleaned themselves with oil and a scraper.

24034.q: What else could you do at the baths besides bathing?
24034.e: Many baths had a sports ground. People also met friends there and shared the latest news.
24034.m: The baths were also a meeting place for sport and chatting.

24035.q: In which Swiss town did even the Romans bathe in hot springs?
24035.e: In Baden in the canton of Aargau, warm water bubbles out of the ground. The Romans called the place Aquae Helveticae and built baths there.
24035.m: Even the Romans bathed in the warm water at Baden.

24036.q: What did most people have to pay to get into the baths?
a: Nothing, only slaves had to pay
24036.e: Entry to the public baths was very cheap. That way even poor people could go bathing.
24036.m: Almost all Romans could afford the baths.

24037.q: Who fought in front of the spectators in the Colosseum?
24037.e: Gladiators were fighters who fought each other to entertain the crowd. Many of them were slaves.

24038.q: What shape is the Colosseum, seen from above?
24038.e: The Colosseum is an amphitheatre. It has the shape of an oval, which is a stretched-out circle.

24039.q: What was under the floor of the arena in the Colosseum?
24039.e: Under the arena there was a network of passages and rooms. Animals and fighters waited there until lifts brought them up.
24039.m: Passages and cages lay under the arena of the Colosseum.

24040.q: Which animals, among others, were shown in the Colosseum?
24040.e: For the animal hunts, wild animals were brought to Rome from many countries. Lions came from Africa, for example.
24040.m: Wild animals such as lions were also shown in the Colosseum.

24041.q: What was stretched over the Colosseum to keep off the sun?
24041.e: Sailors used masts to stretch a giant cloth over the seating. It was called the velarium and gave shade.
24041.m: A huge awning protected the spectators in the Colosseum from the sun.

24042.q: Roughly when was the Colosseum opened?
24042.e: The Colosseum opened in AD 80. That is almost 2000 years ago.
24042.m: The Colosseum is almost 2000 years old.

24043.q: How many storeys does the outer wall of the Colosseum have?
24043.e: The outer wall has three storeys of arches with a fourth, closed storey on top. It is almost 50 metres high.
24043.m: The outer wall of the Colosseum has four storeys.

24044.q: What did the winner of a chariot race receive as a sign of victory?
24044.e: For the Romans the palm branch was a sign of victory. Successful charioteers also often received a lot of money.
24044.m: The winner of a chariot race received a palm branch.

24045.q: Which animals pulled the racing chariots in the Circus Maximus?
24045.e: The light racing chariots were pulled by fast horses. The charioteers stood on the chariot.
24045.m: Horses pulled the Romans’ racing chariots.

24046.q: How many horses pulled a quadriga?
24046.e: The word quadriga comes from the Latin word for four. A quadriga is a chariot with four horses side by side.

24047.q: How many laps did a race in the Circus Maximus usually have?
24047.e: A race usually lasted seven laps. The laps were counted with figures that were turned round or taken down after each lap.
24047.m: A chariot race usually had seven laps.

24048.q: How could you tell the racing teams in the Circus Maximus apart?
a: By the shape of their chariots
24048.e: There were four teams: the Reds, the Whites, the Blues and the Greens. The fans supported their colour, just like in football today.
24048.m: The racing teams in Rome were recognised by their colours.

24049.q: What separated the two sides of the racetrack in the middle?
24049.e: In the middle of the track there was a long wall with statues and columns. The chariots raced around this wall.
24049.m: The chariots raced around a long wall in the middle.

24050.q: Why were the bends particularly dangerous in a chariot race?
a: The ground there was made of stone
Spectators sat on the track there
24050.e: On the tight bends, chariots often crashed into each other or overturned. Such accidents were feared.
24050.m: The tight bends were dangerous in a chariot race.

24051.q: What is the Circus Maximus today?
24051.e: Almost nothing is left of the stands. Today you can see a long grassy field in Rome in the shape of the old racetrack.
24051.m: The Circus Maximus is now a long grassy field in Rome.

24052.q: Which number is the Roman XX?
24052.e: X stands for ten. Two Xs make 10 + 10, which is 20.

24053.q: How do you write the number 3 in Roman numerals?
24053.e: You write the sign I for one three times. 1 + 1 + 1 makes 3.
24053.m: The number three in Roman numerals is III.

24054.q: Which number is the Roman IV?
24054.e: If the smaller sign I comes before the V, you subtract. 5 minus 1 makes 4.

24055.q: Which number is the Roman XII?
24055.e: X is ten and II is two. 10 + 2 makes 12.

24056.e: C stands for a hundred. That fits the Latin word “centum”, meaning a hundred.
24056.m: The Roman C means a hundred.

24057.e: M stands for a thousand. The Latin word for it is “mille”.
24057.m: The Roman M means a thousand.

24058.q: Which number is missing from Roman numerals?
24058.e: The Romans had no sign for zero. This number only came to Europe much later, from India via the Arab world.
24058.m: The Romans had no sign for zero.

24059.q: What does the Latin word “terra” mean?
24059.e: “Terra” means earth or land. The word “terrace” comes from it, for example.

24060.q: What does the Latin word “aqua” mean?
24060.e: “Aqua” means water. Words like aquarium and aquatic come from it.

24061.q: What does the Latin greeting “Salve” mean?
24061.e: The Romans greeted each other with “Salve”. It means something like “Be well” or “Greetings”.
24061.m: The Romans greeted each other with “Salve”.

24062.q: What does the car country code CH stand for?
24062.e: CH is the abbreviation of the Latin name for Switzerland. It means Swiss Confederation.
24062.m: CH stands for the Latin name Confoederatio Helvetica.

24064.q: Which script do we use today that the Romans already had?
24064.e: Our letters A, B, C and so on come from the Romans. We call them the Latin alphabet.
24064.m: Our letters come from the Romans.

24065.q: What does the Latin word “mater” mean?
24065.e: “Mater” means mother. You can hear how similar it is to the English word.

24066.q: What does the Latin word “rex” mean?
24066.e: “Rex” means king. In its earliest times, Rome was ruled by kings.

24067.e: The toga was a long cloth made of wool. It was wrapped skilfully around the body.
24067.m: The toga was a large cloth made of wool.

24068.q: Who was allowed to wear a toga in ancient Rome?
24068.e: The toga was the dress of Roman citizens. Slaves and foreigners were not allowed to wear it.
24068.m: The toga showed that someone was a Roman citizen.

24069.q: What colour was the ordinary toga?
24069.e: The normal toga was white or had the pale colour of undyed wool.

24070.q: What did a Roman wear under the toga?
24070.e: The tunic was a simple shirt-like garment. Many people wore only a tunic for work.
24070.m: A tunic was worn under the toga.

24071.q: What did the toga of boys and high officials have along its edge?
24071.e: This toga was called the toga praetexta. Its edge was decorated with a reddish-purple stripe.
24071.m: Boys wore a toga with a purple stripe.

24072.q: Why did people often need help putting on a toga?
24072.e: The toga was several metres long. So that it fell in nice folds, a slave often helped to drape it.
24072.m: The long toga was hard to put on.

24073.q: What did married Roman women wear instead of a toga?
24073.e: Married Roman women wore a long dress called a stola. They often put a cloak over it.

24074.q: Which modern word comes from the white toga worn by people seeking office?
24074.e: Anyone standing for an office wore a specially white toga. The Latin word “candidus” means shining white.
24074.m: The word candidate comes from the white toga.

24075.q: What was an insula in ancient Rome?
24075.e: An insula was a block of flats with several storeys. Many families lived in it and paid rent.
24075.m: An insula was a Roman block of flats.

24076.q: What does the Latin word “insula” actually mean?
24076.e: “Insula” means island. A block of flats was surrounded by streets, like an island by water.

24077.q: What was on the ground floor of many insulae?
24077.e: Downstairs, facing the street, there were small shops, snack bars and workshops. The flats were above them.
24077.m: There were often shops on the ground floor of an insula.

24078.q: Who usually lived right at the top of an insula?
24078.e: The upper floors were cramped and cheap. People with little money lived there.
24078.m: The poorer people lived right at the top of the insula.

24079.q: Which danger was especially common in the insulae?
24079.e: The houses were partly built of wood and people cooked over open fires. That is why fires broke out often.
24079.m: Fires often broke out in Rome’s blocks of flats.

24080.q: Where did people on the upper floors get their water from?
a: From the fountain in the street
From a pipe in the flat
From a well in the cellar
From a tank on the roof
24080.e: There was no running water upstairs. People carried water up in jugs from the public fountain.
24080.m: In an insula you had to fetch water from the fountain.

24081.q: Why did Emperor Augustus set a maximum height for insulae?
a: Because the temples were meant to be taller
Because the emperor wanted the view
24081.e: Some blocks of flats were badly built and collapsed. So Augustus only allowed buildings up to about 20 metres high.
24081.m: Augustus limited the height of blocks of flats.

24082.q: Where did many residents of an insula go to the toilet?
a: To the cellar of the insula
24082.e: Most flats had no toilet. People went to public latrines, where many sat side by side.

24083.q: Who lived in a Roman villa in the countryside?
24083.e: A villa was a large country house. It belonged to rich families and often had a farm with it.
24083.m: Rich Romans lived in a villa.

24084.q: Where did the Romans usually lay their mosaics?
24084.e: Many mosaics decorated the floors of villas and baths. They last a very long time.
24084.m: The Romans often laid mosaics on the floor.

24085.q: A famous picture made of tiny stones in Pompeii shows a dog. What is written with it?
24085.e: In Latin it says “Cave canem”. The picture shows a dog on a chain.

24086.q: What was the atrium in a Roman house?
24086.e: The atrium was a large hall behind the entrance. There was an opening in the roof that let in light and rain.
24086.m: The atrium was the entrance hall of a Roman house.

24087.q: What was the pool in the middle of the atrium for?
24087.e: Rain fell through the opening in the roof into the pool. The water was collected and used.
24087.m: In the atrium a pool collected rainwater.

24088.q: What was the peristyle in a villa?
24088.e: The peristyle was a garden inside the house. A walkway with columns ran all around it.
24088.m: The peristyle was a garden surrounded by columns.

24089.q: In which Swiss town can you see large Roman mosaics from a villa?
24089.e: Near Orbe in the canton of Vaud, the remains of a large Roman villa were found. Its beautiful mosaics can still be seen today.
24089.m: You can see Roman mosaics in Orbe.

24090.e: The Forum Romanum was the most important square in the city of Rome. People met there, traded and listened to speeches.
24090.m: The Forum Romanum was the main square of Rome.

24091.q: What, among other things, did people do in the Forum Romanum?
24091.e: The Forum had markets, shops and law courts. Politicians gave speeches to the people there.
24091.m: In the Forum people traded and talked.

24092.q: Which buildings stood in the Forum Romanum?
24092.e: Several temples to the Roman gods stood in the Forum, for example one to Saturn.
24092.m: Temples to the gods stood in the Forum Romanum.

24093.q: Where did the Senate meet in the Forum?
24093.e: The Curia was the senators’ meeting house. The building still stands in the Forum today.
24093.m: The Senate met in the Curia.

24094.q: What did the Vestal Virgins have to guard in the Temple of Vesta?
24094.e: The Vestal Virgins were priestesses. They made sure that the sacred fire of the goddess Vesta never went out.
24094.m: The Vestal Virgins guarded the sacred fire.

24095.q: What is a triumphal arch, like the one in the Forum?
24095.e: Triumphal arches were built for victorious generals and emperors. In the Forum, for example, there is the Arch of Titus.
24095.m: A triumphal arch commemorates a victory.

24096.q: What can you see of the Forum Romanum in Rome today?
a: Old columns and remains of walls
24096.e: What is left of the buildings is mainly columns and remains of walls. Today tourists from all over the world visit these ruins.
24096.m: The Forum Romanum is full of ruins today.

24097.q: What was the famous road through the Forum Romanum called?
24097.e: Via Sacra means “Sacred Way”. Triumphal processions passed along it through the Forum.
24097.m: The Via Sacra ran through the Forum Romanum.

24098.e: The hypocaust heated rooms from below. Warm air flowed underneath the floor.
24098.m: The hypocaust was Roman underfloor heating.

24099.q: What was used to make the fire for the hypocaust?
24099.e: Wood was burnt in a furnace outside the room. The hot air then flowed under the floor.
24099.m: The Romans heated the hypocaust with wood.

24100.q: What did the floor above the hypocaust stand on?
24100.e: The floor rested on many small pillars made of bricks. In between there was room for the warm air.
24100.m: In a hypocaust the floor stood on small pillars.

24101.q: After the floor, where else did the warm air flow through?
24101.e: Hollow tiles in the walls carried the warm air upwards. So the walls became warm too.
24101.m: With a hypocaust the walls became warm too.

24102.q: Who usually had to stoke the fire for the hypocaust?
24102.e: The fire had to burn for a long time and be fed with wood all the time. This hard work was usually done by slaves.
24102.m: Slaves kept the fire in the furnace burning.

24103.q: Which buildings often had a hypocaust?
24103.e: The heating was expensive. It was mainly built into baths and the houses of rich people.
24103.m: Baths and villas often had underfloor heating.

24104.q: What does the word hypocaust roughly mean?
24104.e: The word comes from Greek. “Hypo” means under and “kaiein” means to burn or heat.

24105.q: How did rich Romans eat at a banquet?
24105.e: At a fine meal the guests lay on wide couches. This was considered elegant.
24105.m: Rich Romans ate lying down at a banquet.

24106.q: Which side did the guests usually lie on while eating?
24106.e: The guests leaned on their left elbow. That left their right hand free for eating.
24106.m: At a banquet people leaned on their left arm.

24107.q: What did the Romans mainly eat with?
24107.e: The Romans ate a lot with their fingers. There were spoons and knives, but hardly any forks for eating.
24107.m: The Romans mostly ate with their fingers.

24108.q: How many couches usually stood around the table in the dining room?
24108.e: The dining room was called the triclinium. The word means that three couches stood around a table.
24108.m: Three couches stood in the triclinium.

24109.q: Which salty fish sauce did the Romans love?
24109.e: Garum was a salty sauce made from fermented fish. Mulsum was honeyed wine, posca a vinegar drink and puls a porridge.
24109.m: The Romans liked to season food with the fish sauce garum.

24110.q: Who brought the food at a rich family’s banquet?
24110.e: In rich families, slaves served the food and cleared the table. They also brought water for washing hands.
24110.m: Slaves served the guests at a banquet.

24111.q: What did a Roman banquet often start with?
24111.e: The starter was often eggs, olives or salad. At the end there was often fruit.
24111.m: A Roman banquet often began with eggs.

24112.q: What did Roman children often write on at school?
24112.e: A wax tablet was a wooden board with a thin layer of wax. You could write on it and rub it out again.
24112.m: Roman schoolchildren wrote on wax tablets.

24113.q: What did you write with on a wax tablet?
24113.e: The stylus was a pointed stick made of metal, bone or wood. It was used to scratch the letters into the wax.
24113.m: You wrote on a wax tablet with a stylus.

24114.q: What was the flat end of the stylus for?
24114.e: The flat end was used to smooth the wax again. This made the writing disappear.
24114.m: The flat end of the stylus rubbed out the writing.

24115.q: What was the frame of a wax tablet usually made of?
24115.e: The tablets were made of wood. The wax was spread into a hollow in the wood.
24115.m: A wax tablet had a wooden frame.

24116.q: Why were wax tablets handy for practising?
a: They were as light as paper
24116.e: After rubbing out, you could write again. So you did not always need new material.
24116.m: Wax tablets could be used again and again.

24117.q: What was a codex of wax tablets?
24117.e: Several wax tablets were tied together with string. This made a kind of book.
24117.m: Several wax tablets tied together are called a codex.

24118.q: Where in Switzerland were many Roman writing tablets found?
24118.e: The Roman legionary camp of Vindonissa was in Windisch in the canton of Aargau. Many small wooden writing tablets were found there.
24118.m: Many Roman writing tablets were found in Windisch.

24119.q: What did Roman children especially love playing with?
24119.e: Nuts were a popular toy. They were thrown, rolled or stacked in different games.
24119.m: Roman children liked playing with nuts.

24120.q: What did the Roman saying “to leave the nuts behind” mean?
24120.e: When someone grew up, they stopped playing children’s games. So the Romans said they were leaving the nuts behind.
24120.m: For the Romans, “leaving the nuts behind” meant growing up.

24121.q: Roman children threw small pieces like dice. What were they often made of?
24121.e: People used small ankle bones from sheep or goats. They were thrown and caught, a bit like dice.
24121.m: Knucklebones was played with small animal bones.

24122.q: What were Roman dolls made of?
24122.e: Roman dolls were made of clay, wood, bone or cloth. Some even had movable arms and legs.
24122.m: Roman dolls were made of clay or wood.

24123.q: Which toy did Roman children drive along the street with a stick?
24123.e: A hoop made of metal or wood was driven along with a stick. It rolled along beside the child.
24123.m: Roman children drove hoops along with a stick.

24124.q: Which toy spun when you drove it with a whip?
24124.e: Even Roman children knew the spinning top. They kept it moving with a small whip.
24124.m: The spinning top was already popular with Roman children.

24125.q: What else did Roman children like to play?
24125.e: Balls were made of leather and filled with hair or feathers. They were thrown and caught in groups.
24125.m: Roman children liked playing with balls.

24126.q: In which river were the twins Romulus and Remus set adrift in a basket?
24126.e: An evil king had the babies put on the Tiber in a basket. The basket got caught on the bank.
24126.m: The basket with the twins floated on the Tiber.

24127.q: According to legend, who brought up Romulus and Remus after the she-wolf?
24127.e: The shepherd Faustulus found the twins with the she-wolf. He and his wife brought up the boys.
24127.m: A shepherd brought up the twins Romulus and Remus.

24128.q: According to legend, what was the name of the mother of Romulus and Remus?
24128.e: Rhea Silvia was a king’s daughter. Her uncle took the twins away from her because he feared for his power.
24128.m: The mother of Romulus and Remus was called Rhea Silvia.

24129.q: According to legend, in which year was Rome founded?
24129.e: The Romans counted 753 BC as the year their city was founded. The date comes from the legend.
24129.m: According to legend, Rome was founded in 753 BC.

24130.q: According to legend, what happened to Remus when the city wall was being built?
24130.e: The brothers quarrelled over the new city. Remus jumped over the wall, and Romulus killed him.
24130.m: In a quarrel, Romulus killed his brother Remus.

24131.q: According to legend, which god was the father of Romulus and Remus?
a: Neptune, the god of the sea
24131.e: According to legend, Mars, the Roman god of war, was their father. That is why the Romans were seen as children of Mars.
24131.m: According to legend, Mars, the god of war, was the twins’ father.

24132.q: According to legend, how did the brothers decide who would found the city?
24132.e: Each brother stood on a hill and counted vultures in the sky. Romulus saw 12 vultures, Remus only 6.
24132.m: According to legend, the brothers let the birds decide.

24133.q: What is the Capitoline Wolf made of?
24133.e: The Capitoline Wolf is a bronze statue. Bronze is a metal made from copper and tin.
24133.m: The Capitoline Wolf is cast in bronze.

24134.q: In which city is the real Capitoline Wolf?
24134.e: The real statue is in a museum on the Capitoline Hill in Rome. There are copies of it in many places around the world.
24134.m: The Capitoline Wolf is in Rome.

24135.q: Who does the Capitoline Wolf show under her belly?
24135.e: Under the she-wolf sit the twins Romulus and Remus, drinking milk. According to legend, Romulus later founded Rome.
24135.m: Two babies drink milk under the she-wolf.

24136.q: What is the Capitoline Wolf named after?
a: The Capitol, a hill in Rome
24136.e: The Capitol is one of the hills of Rome. The museum with the she-wolf is there.
24136.m: The she-wolf is named after the Capitol in Rome.

24137.q: What are the twins under the Capitoline Wolf called?
24137.e: According to legend, the twins Romulus and Remus were abandoned and fed by a she-wolf. Romulus later founded Rome.
24137.m: Romulus and Remus sit under the she-wolf.

24138.q: What is the she-wolf with the twins a symbol of?
24138.e: The she-wolf with Romulus and Remus recalls the legend of how Rome was founded. You often see it in Rome as an emblem.
24138.m: The she-wolf with the twins is a symbol of Rome.

24139.q: What is the Latin word for she-wolf?
24139.e: Lupa is the Latin word for she-wolf. Ursa means she-bear, vacca cow and aquila eagle.
24139.m: Lupa is the Latin word for she-wolf.

24140.q: According to legend, what did the she-wolf do for the twins?
a: She carried them across the river
She took them to the king
24140.e: The twins were abandoned by the river. A she-wolf found them and gave them milk until a shepherd took them in.
24140.m: According to legend, a she-wolf fed Romulus and Remus with her milk.

24141.q: What was the Senate in ancient Rome?
24141.e: Important and experienced men met in the Senate. They discussed the politics of Rome.
24141.m: In the Senate, important men discussed matters of Rome.

24142.q: Which Latin word does the word “senate” come from?
24142.e: “Senex” means old man in Latin. Mainly older, experienced men sat in the Senate.
24142.m: The Senate was originally a council of elders.

24143.q: What does the “S” in the Roman abbreviation SPQR stand for?
24143.e: SPQR stands for “Senatus Populusque Romanus”. That means “The Senate and People of Rome”.
24143.m: SPQR means the Senate and People of Rome.

24144.e: Senators wore the toga on official occasions. Underneath they wore a tunic with a broad coloured stripe.

24145.q: What colour was the broad stripe on a senator’s tunic?
24145.e: The stripe was purple. Purple was a very expensive dye and showed that someone was important.
24145.m: Senators were recognised by the broad purple stripe on their tunic.

24146.q: What was the building where the Senate in Rome usually met called?
24146.e: The Curia stood in the Forum Romanum. The building still stands there today.
24146.m: The Senate usually met in the Curia.

24147.q: How long did someone usually stay a member of the Roman Senate?
24147.e: Anyone admitted to the Senate usually remained a senator until his death. Only for serious wrongdoing could someone be thrown out.
24147.m: A Roman senator usually stayed in the Senate for life.

24148.q: According to legend, how many senators did Rome have under King Romulus?
24148.e: According to legend, Romulus chose 100 men. They formed the first Senate.
24148.m: According to legend, the first Senate had 100 members.

24149.q: Which city did the general Hannibal come from?
24149.e: Hannibal came from Carthage in North Africa. For a long time Carthage was a great enemy of Rome.

24150.q: Which mountain range did Hannibal cross even before the Alps?
24150.e: Hannibal set off with his army in Spain. First he crossed the Pyrenees, then marched through Gaul to the Alps.

24151.q: In about which year did Hannibal cross the Alps?
24151.e: The crossing of the Alps took place in 218 BC. That was at the start of a long war.
24151.m: Hannibal crossed the Alps in 218 BC.

24152.q: What happened to many of Hannibal’s elephants in the cold Alps?
24152.e: The cold, the snow and hunger were very hard on the elephants. Many animals did not survive.
24152.m: Many of Hannibal’s elephants did not survive the hardships.

24153.q: Which phrase did the Romans cry out in fear when Hannibal was near?
24153.e: “Hannibal ante portas” means “Hannibal is at the gates”. Today the phrase means that danger is very close.
24153.m: Hannibal ante portas means danger is at the door.

24154.q: Who finally defeated Hannibal at the Battle of Zama?
24154.e: In 202 BC the Roman Scipio defeated Hannibal in Africa. That is why Scipio was given the extra name “Africanus”.

24155.q: What were Hannibal’s elephants meant to do in battle?
24155.e: The huge animals made the enemy’s soldiers and horses very afraid. They could break through enemy lines.
24155.m: War elephants were meant to frighten the enemy.

24156.e: Pompeii was a Roman town in southern Italy. Thousands of people lived there.

24157.q: What buried the town of Pompeii in AD 79?
24157.e: When the volcano erupted, ash and small stones fell on the town. Afterwards Pompeii lay metres deep underneath.

24158.q: In which present-day country is Pompeii?
24158.e: Pompeii is in southern Italy, not far from the city of Naples. Today you can visit the ruins.

24159.q: What did researchers in Pompeii use to fill hollow spaces in the ash to show the body shapes of the victims?
24159.e: The victims’ bodies left hollow spaces in the hardened ash. Researchers poured liquid plaster into them and so got exact casts.
24159.m: In Pompeii plaster casts show the shapes of the victims.

24160.q: What are researchers doing in Pompeii today?
a: Rebuilding it as a new town
24160.e: Pompeii has been excavated since about 1748. Houses, streets, pictures and everyday objects are being found.
24160.m: In Pompeii researchers are excavating the old town.

24161.q: Which other Roman town was destroyed in the same volcanic eruption?
24161.e: The town of Herculaneum was buried too. It also lies at the foot of Vesuvius.
24161.m: Herculaneum was also destroyed when Vesuvius erupted.

24162.e: Vesuvius is a volcano in southern Italy. Its eruption in AD 79 destroyed the town of Pompeii.
24162.m: Vesuvius is a volcano in Italy.

24163.q: Which big city is Vesuvius next to?
24163.e: Vesuvius stands on the Bay of Naples. Many people still live at the foot of the mountain today.

24164.e: Vesuvius is still active. Its last eruption was in 1944, and experts watch it closely.
24164.m: Vesuvius could erupt again at any time.

24165.q: Which Roman wrote in letters about how he experienced the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79?
24165.e: Pliny the Younger saw the eruption from the other side of the bay. His letters are among the most important accounts.
24165.m: Pliny the Younger described the eruption of Vesuvius.

24166.q: What comes out of a volcano like Vesuvius when it erupts?
24166.e: In an eruption, hot gases, ash, stones and lava come out of the volcano. Lava is molten rock.
24166.m: A volcano spews out lava and ash.

24167.e: Nero was emperor of Rome from AD 54 to 68. He is one of the best-known emperors.

24168.q: Roughly how old was Nero when he became emperor?
24168.e: Nero became emperor in AD 54. He was only 16 years old at the time.
24168.m: Nero became emperor as a teenager.

24169.q: Which disaster struck Rome in AD 64, when Nero was emperor?
24169.e: In AD 64 a large part of the city of Rome burnt. The fire raged for several days.
24169.m: Rome burnt in AD 64 under Emperor Nero.

24170.q: According to an old story, what did Nero do during the fire of Rome?
24170.e: The story says Nero sang during the fire. Whether this is true is very doubtful, because he was not in Rome when the fire broke out.
24170.m: That Nero sang during the fire is probably just a story.

24171.q: What was the splendid palace that Nero had built after the fire called?
24171.e: In Latin the palace was called the “Domus Aurea”, the Golden House. It was huge and very lavish.
24171.m: Nero had the Golden House built.

24172.q: What did Nero like doing that was unusual for an emperor?
24172.e: Nero loved music and the theatre. He even performed as a singer in front of an audience.
24172.m: Emperor Nero liked performing as a singer.

24173.e: Seneca was a well-known thinker and writer. He taught the young Nero and later advised him.

24174.e: Hadrian was emperor of Rome from AD 117 to 138. He is one of the well-known “good emperors”.

24175.q: What did Emperor Hadrian have on his face that the emperors before him mostly did not?
24175.e: The emperors before Hadrian were mostly clean-shaven. Hadrian wore a beard, and many emperors after him copied him.
24175.m: Hadrian made the full beard popular among Roman emperors.

24177.q: Which famous temple in Rome did Hadrian have rebuilt?
24177.e: The Pantheon has a huge dome with a round hole at the top. Hadrian had it rebuilt.
24177.m: The Pantheon in Rome was rebuilt under Hadrian.

24178.q: What did Emperor Hadrian’s tomb in Rome become?
24178.e: The large round tomb was later turned into a fortress. Today it is called Castel Sant’Angelo.
24178.m: Hadrian’s tomb is now Castel Sant’Angelo.

24179.e: Hadrian’s Wall is a long stone wall. Emperor Hadrian had it built.
24179.m: Hadrian’s Wall is a long wall.

24180.q: In which present-day country is Hadrian’s Wall?
24180.e: Hadrian’s Wall runs right across the north of England. Back then the area was called Britannia.

24181.e: The wall protected the border of the Roman Empire. There the Romans controlled who went in and out.
24181.m: Hadrian’s Wall protected the border of the empire.

24182.q: Roughly how long is Hadrian’s Wall?
24182.e: The wall is about 117 kilometres long. It takes several days to walk its length.
24182.m: Hadrian’s Wall is about 117 kilometres long.

24183.e: Along the wall there were small forts and towers. Roman soldiers lived there and kept watch.

24184.q: Where does Hadrian’s Wall run from and to?
24184.e: The wall runs right across the country, from the west coast to the east coast. So the whole border was closed off.
24184.m: Hadrian’s Wall runs from coast to coast.

24185.q: What extra name does Emperor Constantine have?
24185.e: He is called Constantine the Great. He changed the Roman Empire a great deal.
24185.m: Emperor Constantine is also called Constantine the Great.

24186.q: Which religion did Emperor Constantine especially support?
24186.e: Constantine was the first Roman emperor to support Christianity. Shortly before his death he was baptised.
24186.m: Constantine was the first Christian emperor.

24187.q: Which city did Constantine refound and name after himself?
24187.e: Constantine greatly expanded the old city of Byzantium. He gave it his own name.
24187.m: Constantinople is named after Emperor Constantine.

24188.q: What is the city of Constantinople called today?
24188.e: Constantinople lies on the Bosphorus in present-day Turkey. For a long time now the city has been called Istanbul.

24189.q: In which city did Constantine defeat his rival Maxentius in AD 312?
24189.e: Constantine defeated Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge in Rome. After that he ruled the west of the empire.
24189.m: In AD 312 Constantine defeated Maxentius at Rome.

24190.q: According to the story, what is Constantine said to have seen in the sky before the battle?
24190.e: According to the story, he saw a sign for Christ. He had it painted on his soldiers’ shields.
24190.m: According to the story, Constantine saw a Christian sign in the sky.

24191.q: Which monument in Rome stands next to the Colosseum and recalls Constantine?
24191.e: The Arch of Constantine is a large triumphal arch. It commemorates Constantine’s victory in AD 312.
24191.m: The Arch of Constantine stands by the Colosseum.

24192.q: Which religion did Emperor Constantine support?
a: The religion of the Germanic peoples
24192.e: Constantine allowed Christians to practise their faith freely and had churches built. This made Christianity strong in the Roman Empire.

24193.q: Which day of the week did Constantine make a day of rest in AD 321?
24193.e: Constantine declared Sunday a day of rest. On this day the law courts, for example, were to rest.
24193.m: Constantine made Sunday a day of rest.

24194.e: Marcus Aurelius was emperor of Rome from AD 161 to 180. He is seen as a wise and fair emperor.
24194.m: Marcus Aurelius was a Roman emperor.

24195.q: Apart from being a ruler, what is Emperor Marcus Aurelius especially known as?
24195.e: Marcus Aurelius thought a lot about life. That is why he is often called the “philosopher emperor”.
24195.m: Marcus Aurelius was a philosopher on the imperial throne.

24196.q: What did Marcus Aurelius write down for himself?
24196.e: Marcus Aurelius wrote his thoughts down in a book. It is called the “Meditations” and is still read today.

24197.q: In which language did Marcus Aurelius write his “Meditations”?
24197.e: Although he was a Roman, Marcus Aurelius wrote in Greek. At that time Greek was the language of scholars.
24197.m: Marcus Aurelius wrote his thoughts in Greek.

24198.q: How does the famous bronze statue of Marcus Aurelius in Rome show the emperor?
24198.e: The equestrian statue shows Marcus Aurelius on his horse. Today the original is in the museum on the Capitoline Hill.
24198.m: A famous statue shows Marcus Aurelius on horseback.

24199.q: Why was the equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius not melted down?
24199.e: Many bronze statues were later melted down. This one survived because people believed it showed Emperor Constantine.
24199.m: The statue of Marcus Aurelius survived thanks to a mix-up.

24200.q: On which great river did Marcus Aurelius wage war for a long time against Germanic peoples?
24200.e: On the Danube, Marcus Aurelius fought the Marcomanni and other tribes. He spent many years there.
24200.m: Marcus Aurelius fought for a long time on the Danube.

24201.q: Who became emperor after Marcus Aurelius?
24201.e: After the death of Marcus Aurelius in AD 180, his son Commodus became emperor. Commodus was very different from his father.
24201.m: Commodus succeeded his father Marcus Aurelius.

24202.q: What does the Latin word “testudo” mean?
24202.e: “Testudo” means tortoise. The formation is reminiscent of a tortoise’s hard shell.
24202.m: Testudo is the Latin word for tortoise.

24203.q: Roman soldiers stood close together and then looked like a tortoise. What did they make the shell with?
24203.e: The soldiers held their shields in front of them, beside them and over their heads. This made a shell of shields.
24203.m: In the tortoise, shields form a shell.

24204.q: What did the tortoise formation mainly protect the soldiers from?
24204.e: The shields above their heads kept off arrows, spears and stones. The soldiers underneath stayed protected.
24204.m: The tortoise protected against arrows and stones.

24205.q: Where did the soldiers in the middle of the tortoise hold their shields?
24205.e: The soldiers on the outside held their shields to the side and to the front. The soldiers inside held them like a roof over their heads.
24205.m: In the middle of the tortoise, shields form a roof.

24206.q: How did a tortoise formation move forward?
a: At a run in a wide line
24206.e: All the soldiers had to stay close together so that the shields closed without gaps. That is why the formation moved only slowly.
24206.m: The tortoise moved slowly and tightly packed.

24207.q: When did the Romans like to use the tortoise formation?
a: In horse races in the circus
24207.e: Enemies on the walls shot arrows and threw stones. Under the shields the soldiers could reach the wall safely.
24207.m: The tortoise helped when attacking city walls.

24208.q: What were the Roman foot soldiers who formed the tortoise called?
24208.e: The foot soldiers of the Roman army were called legionaries. They were well trained and often practised the tortoise.
24208.m: Roman foot soldiers were called legionaries.

24209.q: What did the soldiers have to practise a lot for a good tortoise?
24209.e: Only if all the soldiers walked at exactly the same speed did the shields stay close together. Otherwise gaps appeared.
24209.m: For the tortoise everyone had to march in step.

24210.e: The denarius was a coin the Romans paid with. For a long time it was the most important coin in the empire.
24210.m: The denarius was a Roman coin.

24211.q: What metal was the denarius made of?
24211.e: The denarius was a silver coin. Later the Romans mixed in more and more cheaper metal.
24211.m: The denarius was a silver coin.

24212.q: Whose head could often be seen on Roman coins?
24212.e: The emperors had their faces stamped on the coins. That way everyone in the empire knew their ruler.
24212.m: You often see the emperor on Roman coins.

24213.q: What does the Latin word “denarius” mean?
24213.e: At first a denarius was worth 10 small coins called asses. That is why its name means “containing ten”.

24214.q: What was the Roman gold coin called?
24214.e: The aureus was made of gold and worth much more than a denarius. “Aurum” is Latin for gold.
24214.m: The Roman gold coin was called the aureus.

24215.q: Which was worth more for the Romans, a denarius or a sestertius?
24215.e: A sestertius was worth only a quarter of a denarius. Four sestertii made one denarius.
24215.m: A denarius was worth more than a sestertius.

24216.q: Which Roman town near Basel has produced many coin finds?
24216.e: Augusta Raurica is at Augst and Kaiseraugst near Basel. Many coins and a large silver treasure were found there.
24216.m: Many Roman coins were found at Augusta Raurica.

24217.q: Which currency still has a name that comes from the denarius?
24217.e: The dinar is the currency of Serbia, for example. Its name comes from the Roman denarius.
24217.m: The name dinar comes from the Roman denarius.

24218.q: What does the saying “All roads lead to Rome” mean?
a: There are many ways to reach a goal
You must always travel to Rome
There is only one right way
24218.e: The saying means you can reach a goal in different ways. There is not just one right way.
24218.m: All roads lead to Rome means there are many ways to reach a goal.

24219.q: Why did many roads in the Roman Empire lead to Rome?
a: Rome was in the middle of the Alps
Rome was by the North Sea
24219.e: Rome was the capital of the great empire. The Romans built roads from Rome to all the provinces.
24219.m: The Romans built roads from their capital in all directions.

24220.q: What was the top layer of important Roman roads made of?
24220.e: Important Roman roads had large, smooth stone slabs on top. Carts could travel well on them.
24220.m: Roman roads were often paved with stone slabs.

24221.q: What does the Latin word “via” mean?
24221.e: “Via” means way or road in Latin. That is why many Roman roads have the word “Via” in their name.
24221.m: Via is the Latin word for road.

24222.q: How many double steps were there in a Roman mile?
24222.e: Mile comes from the Latin “mille”, which means thousand. A Roman mile had 1000 double steps, which is about 1.5 kilometres.
24222.m: A Roman mile had a thousand double steps.

24223.q: What is the saying “All roads lead to Rome” in French?
a: Tous les chemins mènent à Rome
Toutes les routes sont à Paris
24223.e: The saying exists in many languages. In French it is “Tous les chemins mènent à Rome”.
24223.m: In French too, all roads lead to Rome.

24224.q: Who usually built the roads in the Roman Empire?
24224.e: Soldiers did not only work in war. In peaceful times they built roads, bridges and camps.

24225.q: Which other well-known saying is also about Rome?
a: Rome wasn’t built in a day
Rome was built in one night
24225.e: This saying means that great things take time. So you should be patient.
24225.m: Rome wasn’t built in a day means great things take time.

24226.q: How many wonders of the world were counted in ancient times?
24226.e: Greek writers put together a list of seven especially amazing buildings. We still know this list today.
24226.m: The ancient world had seven wonders.

24227.q: What stone is the Pyramid of Khufu mainly made of?
24227.e: Most of the pyramid is made of limestone blocks. It also used to be covered with pale, smooth limestone slabs.
24227.m: The Pyramid of Khufu is mainly built of limestone.

24228.q: What was the Pyramid of Khufu built for?
a: As a tomb for a pharaoh
24228.e: The pyramid was the tomb of Pharaoh Khufu. It was built about 4500 years ago.
24228.m: The Pyramid of Khufu is the tomb of a pharaoh.

24229.q: Which is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the World?
24229.e: The Pyramid of Khufu is about 2000 years older than the other wonders. It was built about 4500 years ago.
24229.m: The Pyramid of Khufu is the oldest wonder of the world.

24230.q: In which ancient city are the Hanging Gardens said to have been?
24230.e: The Hanging Gardens are said to have been in Babylon in present-day Iraq. Babylon lay on the River Euphrates.
24230.m: The Hanging Gardens are said to have stood in Babylon.

24231.q: Which king is said to have created the Hanging Gardens of Babylon?
24231.e: A legend says that Nebuchadnezzar II had the gardens made for his wife. She is said to have been homesick for green mountains.
24231.m: The Hanging Gardens are credited to King Nebuchadnezzar II.

24232.q: Which wonder of the world is it still unclear really existed?
24232.e: No clear remains of the Hanging Gardens have been found so far. That is why some researchers doubt that they existed.
24232.m: Nobody knows for sure whether the Hanging Gardens really existed.

24233.q: Who did the Colossus of Rhodes show?
a: Zeus, the father of the gods
24233.e: Helios was the protector god of the island of Rhodes. The people built the huge statue in his honour.
24233.m: The Colossus of Rhodes showed the sun god Helios.

24234.q: What metal was the Colossus of Rhodes made of?
24234.e: The statue was made of cast bronze. Inside, iron bars and stones probably held it up.
24234.m: The Colossus of Rhodes was made of bronze.

24235.q: Roughly how tall was the Colossus of Rhodes?
24235.e: The Colossus was about 30 metres tall. That is as high as a building with ten storeys.
24235.m: The Colossus of Rhodes was about 30 metres tall.

24236.q: Where is the island of Rhodes today?
24236.e: Rhodes is a Greek island in the Mediterranean. It lies close to the coast of Turkey.
24236.m: The island of Rhodes belongs to Greece.

24237.q: What destroyed the Colossus of Rhodes?
24237.e: A strong earthquake made the statue fall over. Afterwards it lay on the ground in pieces for a long time.
24237.m: An earthquake brought down the Colossus of Rhodes.

24238.q: Which wonder of the world stood for the shortest time?
24238.e: The Colossus only stood for about 60 years. The other wonders stood for many centuries.
24238.m: The Colossus of Rhodes only stood for a few decades.

24239.q: How did the people of Rhodes pay for the Colossus?
24239.e: An enemy had besieged the city and then withdrawn. The siege machines he left behind were sold to pay for the statue.
24239.m: Selling war equipment paid for the Colossus of Rhodes.

24240.q: Which well-known story about the Colossus is probably not true?
a: It stood astride the harbour entrance
It fell over in an earthquake
24240.e: In many pictures the Colossus stands with its legs apart over the harbour. That would hardly have been technically possible and is seen as a legend.
24240.m: That the Colossus stood over the harbour is just a legend.

24241.q: On which island did the Lighthouse of Alexandria stand?
24241.e: The lighthouse stood on the small island of Pharos in front of the harbour. That is why it is often simply called “the Pharos”.
24241.m: The Lighthouse of Alexandria stood on the island of Pharos.

24242.q: In which present-day country is Alexandria?
24242.e: Alexandria is a large port city in Egypt on the Mediterranean. It was founded by Alexander the Great.

24243.q: Who is the city of Alexandria named after?
24243.e: Alexander the Great founded the city in 331 BC. It still bears his name today.
24243.m: Alexandria bears the name of Alexander the Great.

24244.q: What was the Lighthouse of Alexandria for?
24244.e: At the top a fire burnt that could be seen far out to sea. That way ships found their way safely into the harbour.
24244.m: The lighthouse showed ships the way into the harbour.

24245.q: Roughly how tall was the Lighthouse of Alexandria?
24245.e: It is estimated that the tower was over 100 metres tall. That made it one of the tallest buildings of its time.
24245.m: The Lighthouse of Alexandria was over 100 metres tall.

24246.q: What does the French word “phare” mean?
24246.e: The word recalls the famous lighthouse of Alexandria. In Italian, too, a lighthouse is called “faro”.
24246.m: The island of Pharos gave the lighthouse its French name.

24247.q: What destroyed the Lighthouse of Alexandria?
24247.e: In the Middle Ages several earthquakes badly damaged the tower. In the end only ruins were left.
24247.m: Earthquakes destroyed the Lighthouse of Alexandria.

24248.q: What was later built from the stones of the lighthouse?
24248.e: A sultan had the Citadel of Qaitbay built on the same spot. Stones from the old tower were used for it.
24248.m: A fortress was built from the stones of the lighthouse.

24249.q: Who created the Statue of Zeus at Olympia?
24249.e: Phidias was one of the most famous sculptors in Greece. He created the statue around 430 BC.
24249.m: The sculptor Phidias created the Statue of Zeus.

24250.q: On which Greek peninsula is Olympia?
24250.e: Olympia is in the west of the Peloponnese peninsula in Greece. The famous Statue of Zeus once stood there.
24250.m: Olympia is on the Peloponnese peninsula.

24251.q: How was Zeus shown in the statue at Olympia?
24251.e: Zeus sat on a magnificent throne. If he had stood up, he would have gone through the roof of the temple.
24251.m: The Statue of Zeus showed the god sitting on a throne.

24252.q: Which precious materials decorated the Statue of Zeus?
24252.e: The skin was made of ivory, the robe of gold. Underneath there was a wooden frame.
24252.m: The Statue of Zeus gleamed with gold and ivory.

24253.q: Roughly how tall was the Statue of Zeus?
24253.e: The seated figure was about 12 metres tall. It filled the temple almost up to the ceiling.
24253.m: The Statue of Zeus was about 12 metres tall.

24254.q: What was Olympia famous for in ancient times?
24254.e: Every four years, sports contests were held at Olympia in honour of Zeus. Today’s Olympic Games are named after them.
24254.m: Olympia was the home of the ancient Olympic Games.

24255.q: In which building did the Statue of Zeus stand?
a: In the Temple of Zeus at Olympia
24255.e: A large temple was built at Olympia for the statue. Today only ruins of it can be seen.
24255.m: The Statue of Zeus stood in the Temple of Zeus at Olympia.

24256.q: What did researchers find at Olympia that belongs to the Statue of Zeus?
24256.e: Archaeologists discovered the sculptor’s workshop with tools and moulds. The statue itself is lost.
24256.m: At Olympia the workshop of the sculptor of the Statue of Zeus was found.

24257.q: Which goddess was the temple at Ephesus dedicated to?
24257.e: The huge temple belonged to the goddess Artemis. That is why it was also called the Artemision.
24257.m: The temple at Ephesus was dedicated to the goddess Artemis.

24258.q: What was the goddess Artemis responsible for?
24258.e: Artemis was the goddess of hunting and wild animals. She is often shown with a bow and arrows.
24258.m: Artemis was the goddess of hunting.

24259.q: In which present-day country is Ephesus?
24259.e: The ruins of Ephesus are on the west coast of present-day Turkey. In the past there was a rich Greek city there.

24260.q: What happened to the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus in 356 BC?
a: A man set fire to it to become famous
An earthquake made it sink into the sea
The Romans turned it into a theatre
It was taken to Athens stone by stone
24260.e: A man called Herostratus started a fire because he wanted to become famous at any cost. The temple burnt down and was later rebuilt.
24260.m: Herostratus set fire to the Temple of Artemis to become famous.

24261.q: What destroyed the Temple of Artemis in 356 BC?
24261.e: A man called Herostratus set fire to the temple because he wanted to become famous. Later the temple was rebuilt.
24261.m: The Temple of Artemis was destroyed by fire.

24262.q: What can still be seen of the Temple of Artemis today?
24262.e: Of the more than a hundred columns, only one, which has been put back up, stands today. The rest lies in ruins.
24262.m: Only one column of the Temple of Artemis stands today.

24263.q: What stone was the Temple of Artemis built from?
24263.e: The temple was one of the first large buildings made entirely of marble. That made it especially splendid.
24263.m: The Temple of Artemis was built of marble.

24264.q: Which rich king helped build the first great Temple of Artemis?
24264.e: King Croesus of Lydia was famous for his wealth. He donated columns for the temple.
24264.m: The rich King Croesus helped build the Temple of Artemis.

24265.q: Who was the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus built for?
24265.e: The Mausoleum was the tomb of King Mausolus. He died in 353 BC.
24265.m: The Mausoleum was the tomb of King Mausolus.

24266.q: What was the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus?
24266.e: The dead king lay in this splendid building. It was a huge, decorated tomb.
24266.m: The Mausoleum at Halicarnassus was a tomb.

24267.q: What does the word “mausoleum” mean today?
24267.e: Because the tomb of Mausolus was so famous, splendid tomb buildings are called mausoleums today. The word comes from the king’s name.
24267.m: A mausoleum is a large tomb.

24268.q: What stood right at the top of the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus?
24268.e: On the top of the tomb stood a stone chariot with four horses. Parts of it can be seen in a museum today.
24268.m: A chariot with four horses stood on top of the Mausoleum.

24269.q: What is the city of Halicarnassus called today?
24269.e: Halicarnassus is today’s town of Bodrum. It lies on the coast of Turkey.

24270.q: Roughly how tall was the Mausoleum?
24270.e: The tomb was about 45 metres tall. At the top stood a stone chariot with four horses.
24270.m: The Mausoleum was about 45 metres tall.

24271.q: What did knights later use many stones from the Mausoleum for?
24271.e: The Knights of St John built a castle in Bodrum. For it they took stones from the crumbling Mausoleum.
24271.m: Knights built a castle with stones from the Mausoleum.

24272.q: In which museum are many figures from the Mausoleum today?
a: The Swiss National Museum in Zurich
24272.e: In the 19th century researchers brought statues and reliefs to England. Today they are on display in the British Museum.
24272.m: Many figures from the Mausoleum are in the British Museum in London.

24273.q: In which city was the most famous library of the ancient world?
24273.e: The Library of Alexandria was the largest collection of books in the ancient world. It stood in Egypt.
24273.m: The most famous library of the ancient world was in Alexandria.

24274.q: What were the texts in the Library of Alexandria written on?
24274.e: The texts were on long scrolls of papyrus. Books with pages like today did not exist yet.
24274.m: In Alexandria the texts were on papyrus scrolls.

24275.e: Papyrus is a plant that grows by the Nile. Sheets for writing on were made from its stems.
24275.m: Papyrus is made from a plant from the Nile.

24276.q: In which country was the Library of Alexandria?
24276.e: Alexandria is in Egypt on the Mediterranean. Greek kings founded the library there more than 2000 years ago.
24276.m: The Library of Alexandria was in Egypt.

24277.q: What happened to books on ships that came to Alexandria?
24277.e: Books on arriving ships were taken and copied. The library often kept the original and gave back a copy.
24277.m: Alexandria had books from ships copied.

24278.q: Which scholar from the library calculated the circumference of the Earth?
24278.e: Eratosthenes ran the library. He measured shadows in two places and from this calculated the Earth’s circumference quite accurately.
24278.m: Eratosthenes calculated the circumference of the Earth in Alexandria.

24279.q: Does the old Library of Alexandria still exist today?
a: Yes, it is still completely standing
Yes, about half of it still stands
No, but all the scrolls survive
24279.e: The library was gradually destroyed by fires and wars. None of the scrolls have survived.
24279.m: The old Library of Alexandria is lost.

24280.e: The Bibliotheca Alexandrina recalls the famous old library. It is a modern library with room for millions of books.
24280.m: Since 2002 Alexandria has had a large library again.

24281.q: In which present-day country are the ruins of Carthage?
24281.e: Carthage lay on the Mediterranean. Today the ruins are near the capital, Tunis.

24282.q: Which people founded the city of Carthage?
24282.e: Seafarers from Phoenicia founded Carthage on the coast of North Africa. From there they traded across the whole Mediterranean.

24283.q: According to legend, which queen founded Carthage?
24283.e: The legend tells of Queen Dido, who fled from her homeland. She founded Carthage on a foreign coast.
24283.m: According to legend, Queen Dido founded Carthage.

24284.q: Who won the wars between Rome and Carthage in the end?
24284.e: After three wars Rome won. In 146 BC the Romans destroyed Carthage.
24284.m: In the end Rome defeated Carthage.

24285.q: What are the wars between Rome and Carthage called?
24285.e: The Romans called the Carthaginians “Punici”. That is why the wars are called the Punic Wars.
24285.m: The wars between Rome and Carthage are called the Punic Wars.

24286.q: Which general from Carthage crossed the Alps with elephants?
24286.e: In 218 BC Hannibal crossed the Alps with his army and war elephants. He wanted to attack Rome from the north.
24286.m: Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants.

24287.e: Carthage was on the north coast of Africa. From there it was not far to Sicily.

24288.q: In which year did the Romans destroy Carthage?
24288.e: At the end of the Third Punic War the Romans captured the city and destroyed it. Later they built a Roman city there.

24289.q: How did the Carthaginians mainly make their living?
a: From raising livestock in the mountains
24289.e: Carthage had a large harbour and many ships. The traders carried goods across the whole Mediterranean.
24289.m: Carthage grew rich through trade across the sea.

24290.q: On which island is the palace of Knossos?
24290.e: Knossos is on Crete, the largest island in Greece. The Minoans lived there.
24290.m: The palace of Knossos is on Crete.

24291.q: Which legendary king is the culture of Knossos named after?
24291.e: The culture on Crete is called the Minoan culture. The name comes from the legendary King Minos.
24291.m: The Minoan culture is named after King Minos.

24292.q: According to legend, who built the labyrinth for King Minos?
24292.e: Daedalus was a brilliant inventor and builder. Later he escaped from Crete with his son Icarus on wings.
24292.m: The inventor Daedalus built the labyrinth.

24293.q: What is special about the red columns in the palace of Knossos?
a: They get narrower towards the bottom
They get narrower towards the top
They are twisted like a rope
24293.e: The red wooden columns are wider at the top than at the bottom. That is exactly the opposite of Greek temples.
24293.m: The columns at Knossos get narrower towards the bottom.

24294.q: Roughly how old are the remains of the palace of Knossos?
24294.e: The palace was built in the Bronze Age and rebuilt several times. It was at its height about 3500 years ago.
24294.m: The palace of Knossos is about 3500 years old.

24295.q: What helped Theseus find his way out of the labyrinth?
24295.e: The king’s daughter gave him a thread. He unwound it and followed it back to the exit.
24295.m: Theseus found his way out of the labyrinth with a thread.

24296.q: Apart from excavating, what did the Englishman Arthur Evans do at Knossos?
a: He rebuilt parts of the palace
He built a hotel in the ruins
He took the whole palace to London
24296.e: Evans excavated the palace from 1900. He had some parts rebuilt with concrete and painted, which is controversial today.
24296.m: Arthur Evans rebuilt parts of Knossos.

24297.q: Which animal can be seen in many pictures at Knossos?
24297.e: In wall paintings young people leap over bulls. The bull was an important animal on Crete.
24297.m: The bull can be seen in many pictures at Knossos.

24298.q: In which present-day country did the Etruscans live?
24298.e: The Etruscans lived in central Italy. They were at their height before Rome became powerful.
24298.m: The Etruscans lived in present-day Italy.

24299.q: Which present-day region of Italy is named after the Etruscans?
24299.e: The Romans also called the Etruscans “Tusci”. The name Tuscany comes from this.
24299.m: Tuscany is named after the Etruscans.

24300.q: Which city was ruled by Etruscan kings in its early days?
24300.e: The last kings of Rome were Etruscans. After the last king, Rome became a republic.
24300.m: In its early days Rome was ruled by Etruscan kings.

24301.q: What did the Etruscans often decorate with paintings?
24301.e: The Etruscans built burial chambers like small houses. The walls are painted with cheerful pictures of feasts and dances.
24301.m: The Etruscans painted pictures in their tombs.

24302.q: What is special about the language of the Etruscans?
a: It is still not fully understood today
It is the same as Latin
24302.e: Etruscan writing can be read because it is similar to the Greek alphabet. But many words are still not understood today.
24302.m: The Etruscan language has still not been fully deciphered.

24303.q: Which people in the Alps probably had a language related to Etruscan?
24303.e: The Raetians lived in places including what is now the Grisons. Their language was probably related to Etruscan.
24303.m: The Raetian language was probably related to the Etruscan language.

24304.q: What were the Etruscans especially skilled at?
24304.e: The Etruscans made artistic figures, mirrors and vessels from bronze. A famous example is the Chimera of Arezzo.
24304.m: The Etruscans were skilled bronze casters.

24305.q: What did Etruscan priests examine to predict the future?
24305.e: The priests read the will of the gods from the livers of sacrificed animals. A bronze model of such a liver was found near Piacenza.
24305.m: Etruscan priests read the future from animals’ livers.

24306.q: Which people took over a lot from the Etruscans?
24306.e: The Romans lived right next to the Etruscans. They took over religious customs and symbols of power, for example.
24306.m: The Romans took over a lot from the Etruscans.

24307.q: Which people built the rock city of Petra?
24307.e: The Nabataeans were a trading people from Arabia. Petra was their capital.
24307.m: The Nabataeans built the rock city of Petra.

24308.q: How were the buildings of Petra built?
a: They were carved into the rock
They were built of mud bricks
They were built of marble blocks
24308.e: The facades were chiselled straight out of the rock walls. That is why Petra is called a rock city.
24308.m: In Petra the buildings were carved into the rock.

24309.q: What colour is the rock of Petra?
24309.e: Petra is carved from reddish sandstone. That is why it is also called the “rose-red city”.
24309.m: The rock of Petra glows reddish.

24310.q: What is the most famous building in Petra called?
24310.e: In Arabic the Treasury is called Khazne al-Firaun. A legend told of a treasure in the urn at the top of the facade.
24310.m: The Treasury of the Pharaoh is the most famous building in Petra.

24311.q: How do you get into the city of Petra on foot?
24311.e: The way leads through the Siq, a narrow rocky gorge. At the end you suddenly see the Treasury.
24311.m: A narrow gorge leads into the rock city of Petra.

24312.q: Which Swiss city did the explorer come from who discovered Petra for Europe in 1812?
24312.e: Johann Ludwig Burckhardt came from a Basel family and grew up in Basel. He travelled through the region in disguise and in 1812 became the first European in a long time to see Petra.
24312.m: Johann Ludwig Burckhardt from Basel discovered Petra for Europe.

24313.q: Which list was Petra voted onto in 2007?
a: The New Seven Wonders of the World
24313.e: In a worldwide vote in 2007, Petra became one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. It has also been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1985.
24313.m: Since 2007 Petra has been one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.

24314.q: In which present-day country are the ruins of Troy?
24314.e: Troy lies on a hill in north-west Turkey. The hill is called Hisarlik.
24314.m: The ruins of Troy are in Turkey.

24315.q: Which poet told of the war over Troy?
24315.e: The Greek poet Homer described the war in a long poem. The work is almost 3000 years old.
24315.m: Homer told of the war over Troy.

24316.q: What is Homer’s work about the war over Troy called?
24316.e: The Iliad tells of part of the war over Troy. The name comes from “Ilion”, another name for Troy.
24316.m: Homer’s work about Troy is called the Iliad.

24317.q: Who was Paris in the legend of Troy?
24317.e: Paris was a son of the king of Troy. He carried off a queen from Greece and so started the war.
24317.m: Paris was a prince of Troy.

24318.q: What did researchers find in the hill of Troy?
a: Many cities on top of each other
24318.e: The remains of many settlements lie on top of each other in the hill. Again and again, people built anew on the ruins.
24318.m: Many cities lie on top of each other in the hill of Troy.

24319.q: What did Heinrich Schliemann want to find?
24319.e: Schliemann believed that Homer’s stories were true. So he searched for the city from the legend.
24319.m: Heinrich Schliemann searched for the city of Troy.

24320.q: Which country did Heinrich Schliemann come from?
24320.e: Schliemann was born in 1822 in Mecklenburg in Germany. He became very rich as a merchant.

24321.q: How did Heinrich Schliemann first earn his money?
24321.e: Schliemann became rich through trading. He later used this money to pay for his excavations.
24321.m: Schliemann became rich as a merchant.

24322.q: What did Schliemann find at Troy in 1873?
24322.e: Schliemann called the find “Priam’s Treasure”, after the king of Troy. Later it turned out that the treasure is much older.
24322.m: Schliemann found a gold treasure at Troy.

24323.q: Where did Schliemann find a famous golden death mask?
24323.e: At Mycenae in Greece, Schliemann excavated royal tombs. He called one gold mask the “Mask of Agamemnon”.
24323.m: Schliemann found a golden death mask at Mycenae.

24324.q: Which site on Lake Neuchâtel is a period of the Celts named after?
24324.e: At La Tène near Marin, a great many Celtic weapons and pieces of jewellery were found. That is why the late Celtic period is called the La Tène period.
24324.m: A period of the Celts is named after La Tène.

24325.q: Where did the Helvetii mainly live?
24325.e: The Helvetii lived mainly in the Plateau between the Jura and the Alps. There was good land for fields and livestock there.
24325.m: The Helvetii lived mainly in the Plateau.

24326.e: An oppidum was a large settlement with walls or ramparts. The Celts often built them on hills or by rivers.
24326.m: An oppidum was a protected Celtic settlement.

24327.q: Which Roman general defeated the Helvetii at Bibracte?
24327.e: In 58 BC Caesar defeated the Helvetii at Bibracte in Gaul. After that they had to return to their homeland.
24327.m: Caesar defeated the Helvetii at Bibracte.

24328.q: Which river flows around the peninsula in Bern where the Helvetii had a large settlement?
24328.e: In Bern the Aare forms several loops. On the Enge peninsula there was a fortified settlement of the Helvetii, and later a small Roman settlement too.
24328.m: In Bern the Helvetii settled in a loop of the Aare.

24329.q: What did the Helvetii want to do in 58 BC?
a: Build a wall around the Alps
24329.e: The Helvetii burnt their villages and wanted to look for new land to the west in Gaul. Caesar stopped them.
24329.m: In 58 BC the Helvetii wanted to emigrate to Gaul.

24330.q: What was the name of a famous leader of the Helvetii?
24330.e: Divico led the Helvetii against the Romans. Even as a young man he had defeated a Roman army.
24330.m: Divico was a leader of the Helvetii.

24331.q: What did the Helvetii pay with when trading?
24331.e: The Helvetii had their own metal coins. In 1890 a large lump made of such coins was even found in Zurich.

24332.q: In which year did the Helvetii leave their homeland?
24332.e: In 58 BC the Helvetii set off westwards. That was over 2000 years ago.

24333.q: Which Roman general stood in the way of the Helvetii in 58 BC?
24333.e: Julius Caesar was governor in Gaul at the time. He did not want the Helvetii to march through Roman territory.

24334.q: According to Caesar, what did the Helvetii do with their villages before they left?
24334.e: According to Caesar, the Helvetii set fire to their houses. That way they could not simply turn back.
24334.m: The Helvetii burnt down their villages before leaving.

24335.q: Where did the Helvetii want to go when they left?
24335.e: The Helvetii wanted to go to the west of Gaul, in present-day France. The Santones tribe lived there.
24335.m: The Helvetii wanted to move west.

24336.q: Near which place were the Helvetii defeated in 58 BC?
24336.e: At Bibracte in Gaul the Helvetii lost a great battle. Bibracte is in present-day France.
24336.m: The Helvetii were defeated at Bibracte.

24337.q: What did the Helvetii have to do after their defeat?
24337.e: The victor sent the Helvetii back to their old territory. There they were to rebuild their villages.
24337.m: After their defeat the Helvetii went home.

24338.q: According to Caesar, how many villages did the Helvetii burn when they left?
24338.e: Caesar writes of about 400 villages and twelve fortified towns. But researchers have found only a few traces of fire.
24338.m: According to Caesar, about 400 villages were burnt.

24339.q: What did the Helvetii take with them when they left?
24339.e: According to Caesar, whole families set off with carts and animals. Today, however, researchers doubt his high numbers.
24339.m: Whole families went along when the Helvetii left.

24340.e: Divico was a famous Celtic leader. He lived over 2000 years ago.
24340.m: Divico was a leader of the Helvetii.

24341.q: Against whom did Divico win a battle in 107 BC?
24341.e: Divico defeated a Roman army under the general Lucius Cassius Longinus. That was a great success for his people.

24342.q: Against whom did the Helvetian leader Divico win a famous battle?
24342.e: In 107 BC Divico defeated a Roman army in what is now France.

24343.q: Roughly how old was Divico in 58 BC?
24343.e: Divico was born around 130 BC. So in 58 BC he was already an old man.
24343.m: In 58 BC Divico was already an old man.
